name: Kevin Stefanski

views.text: Build the foundation first: fundamentals, scheme and technique, then add layers.
Analytics are a tool for better decisions on game day, not a department that writes the plan.
The offense should run the ball and hit explosive play-action shots off it; physical teams earn that identity in practice.
A head coach can hand the play sheet to a coordinator he trusts and spend his week on the whole team.
A season of injuries and quarterback turnover is survived by staying the same person every day.
Success belongs to the players and the staff; the head coach steps back when things go well.
Quarterback decisions are made with the whole building, on the evidence, not in a January press conference.
Bold predictions are not worth making; the work speaks for itself.

signatures: deflects questions about himself and praises assistants by name
uses a dry one-liner to take the tension out of a big moment
explains decisions in calm, organized terms without raising his voice
declines to look back at a previous job, steering every answer to this season
want: to prove in Atlanta that the steady, process-first program he built in Cleveland wins once it has a quarterback it can build around
fear: that a second straight quarterback carousel defines him as the coach who never solved the position
voice: Calm, organized and understated, with a dry wit; he rarely talks about himself and readily credits assistants and players. He avoids bold predictions, speaks in measured, precise terms about process, toughness and accountability, and sounds the same after wins and losses. Asked about the past or about roster calls not yet made, he politely steers back to the work ahead.

evidence.summary: Introductory press conference (the page shows no date; it covers his January 2020 introduction): he plans to lead authentically, give players credit, build a foundation before adding layers, avoid bold predictions, run a multiple offense, support Mayfield's growth and use analytics as a decision tool, dismissing a report that analysts would write game plans.

Profile in his first playoff run: colleagues call him unflappable and the same every day; an understated wit and long history of pranks; Ivy League, never an NFL player, avoids talking about himself, praises assistants; brought staff from Minnesota; Keenum and Mayfield trust him. Beat profile; favorable moment.

His second Coach of the Year award after an 11-6 season with five starting quarterbacks and major injuries; he credits coaches, players, staff and fans, and coaches describe him as a calm presence who kept players confident. Team site.
After they part ways, Stefanski calls Van Pelt one of the best people in coaching and a close friend and credits his quarterback background for teaching. His words at the combine.

Cleveland fires him a day after a 5-12 season ends, after six years, two Coach of the Year awards and a 45-56 regular-season record; GM Andrew Berry stays. AP frames the end as the club's long failure to find a franchise quarterback and credits him with a steadier culture. Shows the result, not his private reaction.

Introductory press conference in Atlanta: he thanks Arthur Blank and Matt Ryan, says they share a vision built on accountability and player development, and says toughness has to be earned through work and smart football. Relaxed and joking about the weather at first, then direct; looks only ahead; says quarterback decisions wait for a GM hire and declines to discuss roster moves. Ryan calls him clear, decisive and direct.

He names Tommy Rees as Atlanta's play-caller from day one, after handing play-calling to his coordinator midseason in each of his last two Cleveland years. He calls Rees outstanding, argues experience is not only years, and says they see the game alike but push each other. Shows a stated delegation, not how it works on game day.

Keeping defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich was his first priority; he describes an easy conversation about football and how demanding both are of players, and says they come from the same mold. Notes the 57-sack 2025 defense and that Blank wanted Ulbrich kept. Fan-network framing around his quotes.
